replying_to: Replying to Treatment effect estimation with confounder balanced instrumental variable regression
display_title: Official Review of Paper304 by Reviewer a5qb

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a new instrumental variable regression method for treatment effects estimation in the presence of unmeasured confounders. There are a few contributions of the work. First, it combines the instrumental variable regression with confounder balancing. Second, it relaxes the additive noise assumption.
content.main_review:
This paper improves existing instrumental variable (IV) regression methods for treatment effects estimation by incorporating confounders balancing. Although the idea is simple, the proposed method shows competitive performance compared with existing approaches. The following are my comments.

1. In this paper, the authors proposed to learn a representation of confounders based on Wasserstein distance. What is the motivation to use the Wasserstein distance? What are the advantages of this approach compared with existing approaches based on integral probability metrics or mutual information? In addition, is there theoretical guarantee that the learned representation $C$ is independent of $\hat{T}$? 

2. The theoretical optimality of the proposed approach compared with IV regression methods without confounders balancing and/or confounders balancing methods without IV regression is not discussed. In addition, the asymptotic distribution of the proposed estimator for average treatment effect estimation and its associated variance estimation are not discussed.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the proposed method makes a useful contribution to the literature of treatment effect estimation with unmeasured confounders. Even though from a higher level, the proposed method is not truly innovative, it has its value and demonstrates superior performance compared with many existing approaches for treatment effect estimation in the presence of unmeasured confounders.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer a5qb Comments
content.comment:
Thank you for your thought-provoking comment. We detail our response below and have corrected corresponding part in our revision. We would really appreciate it if you could let us know if you have any further concerns.

**About the concerns of the Wasserstein distance**: 

In fact, the confounder balancing baselines such as CFR (Shalit et al., 2017), DR-CFR (Hassanpour and Greiner, 2019b) adopt Wasserstein distance (Wass) to calculate the dissimilarity of distributions from different treatment arms and fit a balanced representation by minimizing the discrepancy. For the sake of fairness, we uniformly use Wass distance as the discrepancy metrics for CFR, DR-CFR, and CB-IV in the experimental comparison. 

In addition, for some function families, there is no known way or a simple method to compute the integral probability metric or its gradients efficiently. Wass distance has consistent estimators, which can be efficiently computed in the finite sample case (Shalit et al., 2017; Sriperumbudur et al., 2012). Besides, Wass distance ($W_\mathrm{p}(\mu, \nu) \stackrel{\text { def }}{=}\left(\inf _\mathrm{\pi \in \Pi(\mu, \nu)} \int_\mathrm{\Omega^{2}} D(x, y)^{p} d \pi(x, y)\right)^{1 / p}, p \in[1, \infty)$) is a common measure in deep learning, and many algorithm breakthroughs (Arjovsky et al., 2017; Cuturi & Doucet, 2014) benefit from it. It has many favorable properties, documented both in theory (Villani, 2009; Cuturi and Doucet, 2014b) and practice (Rubner et al., 1997; Pele and Werman, 2009). 

In this paper, we adopt the Wass distance in binary treatment cases for fairness and expect better performance and choose mutual information minimization (Cheng et al. 2020) in continuous treatment cases. In binary treatment cases, $\mathbb{P}(C|T=0)=\mathbb{P}(C|T=1)$ if and only if $IPM=Wass(C_{T=0},C_{T=1})=0$. Obviously, in this case, $IPM=0$ means that the distributions of representation $C$ are the same in the treated group and the control group, i.e., $\mathbb{P}(C|T=0)=\mathbb{P}(C|T=1)=\mathbb{P}(C)$. The learned representation $C$ is independent of $T$. In continuous treatment cases, we can regard the minimization of mutual information between representation $C$ and treatment $T$ as $C \perp T$.

**About the theoretical optimality**: Shalit et al. (2017) give a novel and intuitive generalization-error bound showing that the expected treatment effect estimation error is bounded by the standard generalization-error and the distance between the treated and control distributions induced by the representation: 
$\epsilon(h, \theta) \leq 2\left(\epsilon_{F}^{t=0}(h, \theta)+\epsilon_{F}^{t=1}(h, \theta)+B_{\theta} I P M_{\mathrm{G}}\left(p_{\theta}^{t=1}, p_{\theta}^{t=0}\right)-2 \sigma_{Y}^{2}\right)$
where $\epsilon_{F}^{T=t}(h, \theta)=\int_{\mathcal{X}} \ell_{2}(y, h(T=t,f_\theta(x))) p^{T=t}(x) d x$ for $t \in \{0,1\}$; $p^{T=t}(x)$ denotes the PDF of $x$ given $T=t$; $p_\mathrm{\theta}^{T=t}=\{f_\mathrm{\theta(x_i)}\}_\mathrm{i:t_i=t}$; $B_\mathrm{\theta}$ is a constant; $ \sigma_\mathrm{Y}^{2}$ is the expected variance of $Y$. 

Based on the two-stage regression of IV methods, we use $\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{2}$ (Eq. 17) as the loss function in the outcome regression stage: $\min_\mathrm{\theta, \xi^0, \xi^1} \mathcal{L}_\mathrm{2}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_\mathrm{i=1}^n (y_i-\sum_\mathrm{\hat{t} \in \{0,1\}} h_\mathrm{\xi^{\hat{t}}}(f_\theta(x_i)) \hat{P}(\hat{t} \mid z_i, x_i) )^2 + \alpha \text{ disc}(\hat{t}, f_\theta(x_i)) $. In mathematical, the optimization goal $\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{2}$ is consistent with the error bound $\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{2}=2(\epsilon_\mathrm{F}^{t=0}(h, \theta)+\epsilon_\mathrm{F}^{t=1}(h, \theta)+B_\mathrm{\theta} I P M_\mathrm{\mathrm{G}}\left(p_\mathrm{\theta}^{t=1}, p_\mathrm{\theta}^{t=0}\right)-2 \sigma_\mathrm{Y}^{2})$. We bound the error $\epsilon(h, \theta)$ by minimizing $\epsilon_\mathrm{F}^{t=0}(h, \theta)+\epsilon_\mathrm{F}^{t=1}(h, \theta)$ and $I P M_\mathrm{\mathrm{G}}\left(p_\mathrm{\theta}^{t=1}, p_\mathrm{\theta}^{t=0}\right)$ simultaneously. Combining with IV methods and confound balance methods, we eliminate the confounding bias from unmeasured confounders and adjust the observed confounders.

**About the asymptotic properties**: In this paper, we mainly focus on treatment effect estimation and have not examined statistical inference yet. Inference after deep neural network training is generally very challenging (Max Farrell, Tengyuan Liang, Sanjog Misra. Deep Neural Networks for Estimation and Inference. Econometrica, 2021). We leave this to future exploration. 

**We have updated the paper to address your concerns; see the modified parts, marked in red**:

(i) About the Wass distance: We add it in Section G.2 in Appendix on pages 20-21; 

(ii) About the Error bound: We add it in Section G.3 in Appendix on page 21; 

Please forward any other thoughts, ideas, or concerns.

replying_to: Replying to Treatment effect estimation with confounder balanced instrumental variable regression
display_title: Official Review of Paper304 by Reviewer uVdE

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a confounder balanced IV regression (CB-IV) algorithm to estimate average treatment effects (ATEs) in the setup of instrumental variable (IV) regression. The CB-IV algorithm is essentially a two-stage representation learning method with instrumental variables. The implementation process is similar to the classic two-stage least-squares regression method for IV regression. The first stage is to regress the treatment variable onto the instrumental variable and observed confounders. In the second stage, the authors propose to regress the outcome variable onto the predicted treatment variable and observed covariates while balancing the representation of the observed covariates between the treated and control group. The proposed algorithm shows strong performances in extensive simulation.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

This paper does an excellent job of reviewing the literature in IV and balanced representation learning. It is clear what are the limitations of the existing methods and applying the proposed method can potentially lead to some improvements. The paper shows an interesting identification formula for treatment effects when the learnt representation is independent of the predicted treatment variable. The authors use both synthetic and real-world datasets to validate the proposed method. Overall, the paper is well-written and easy to follow, e.g., the assumptions and proposed method are all well stated.

Weaknesses:

As you mentioned in Section 2.1, there is a trade-off in learning balanced representations. In fact, if the sample size is large, I don’t see any point in learning balanced representations because we can estimate the control and treated outcome well enough for any value of the observed covariates. If we still try to balance the representations, the representations will lose information predictive of the predicted treatment variable. This information is often also the information predictive of the outcome. In other words, learning balanced representations can increase the bias of treatment effects estimation. In finite samples, learning balanced representations can be seen as a kind of regularization on the outcome regression model. Its gain is from decreasing the estimator variance at the price of increasing the bias. The authors mention a few times in the paper balanced representations remove the confounding bias from the observed confounders, which is the opposite of what I think. A more complete and clear story of the bias-variance trade-off should be provided in this paper.

In the simulation studies, the authors only compare with deep IV methods. Could you also compare your method with the kernel-based IV methods e.g., [Singh et al., 2019; Muandet et al., 2019]? In Figure 2, we don’t see any performance improvement as the sample size increases. The proposed method already does very well in small sample sizes on average.  The balanced representation methods without using IV perform much better than the pure IV based methods. Could we adjust or increase the difficulty of the simulation so that there are clear trends of the results and using the instrumental variable also becomes more important? Finally, I don’t get why OneSIV, the ablation version of CB-IV, has worse performance as the sample size increases.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposes a simple method for instrumental regression levering the recent technique of balanced representation learning in causal inference. I feel the paper has room for improvement regarding the simulation studies and the bias discussion of balanced representation. I keep my score slightly lower than acceptance. I will adjust my score according to the authors’ responses to my comments.

$$ $$
______________________________________________________________________________________________________

I thank the authors for addressing my comments. I increase my score to 6.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper304 by Reviewer uVdE

content.title: Response to Reviewer uVdE Comments (Part 1)
content.comment:
We sincerely appreciate your constructive comments to improve our paper. Below, we address your concerns point by point. Please kindly let us know whether you have any further concerns.

**About the direct regression and confounder balance**: Thank your suggestive comments. As for the concern on the balanced representations, we agree with you that learning balanced representation would increase the bias of treatment effect, but it can help to reduce the variance due to imbalanced treated and control group distributions and hence to achieve better bias-variance trade-off (Shalit et al., 2017). We have corrected this part from “reduce bias” to “achieve better bias-variance trade-off” through our paper. As you suggested, in finite samples, our balanced representation (by learning representation with reducing Wasserstein distance between treated and control) can be seen as a type of regularization on the regression model and enabling a new type of bias-variance trade-off. Overall, our algorithm is seeking a balanced representation $C=f_{\theta}(X)$ and regression hypothesis $h(\cdot)$ that minimize a trade-off between predictive accuracy and imbalance in the representation space with the objective function in Eq. (17). 

As for the direct regression model, we agree with you that one can estimate the control and treated outcome well enough if the training sample size is large enough and unbiased. In practice, however, the collected data is always finite and has confounding bias (the distribution of confounders X might differ between treated and control groups). Then the direct regression might be incorrect or overfitted on the limited biased data. Moreover, the treatment indicator might be get lost in direct regression due to the high-dimensional confounders. In this paper, we propose to balance the representation to reduce the estimation variance and hence to achieve better bias-variance trade-off (Shalit et al., 2017), and avoid the loss of treatment information.

Extensive experimental results demonstrated that with learning balanced representation, our CB-IV method achieved better performance than previous IV methods (such as DeepIV, KernelIV, DualIV and OneSIV) with direct regression. Moreover, the balanced representation in our algorithm can bound the expected treatment effect estimation error like (Shalit et al., 2017): $\epsilon(h, \Phi) \leq 2\left(\epsilon_{F}^{t=0}(h, \Phi)+\epsilon_{F}^{t=1}(h, \Phi)+B_{\Phi} I P M_{\mathrm{G}}\left(p_{\Phi}^{t=1}, p_{\Phi}^{t=0}\right)-2 \sigma_{Y}^{2}\right)$. "Balanced" representation means that the gain is from decreasing the bias and variance of the population, including the bias of counterfactual estimation, at the price of a small increase in the estimation bias of common samples in data (We details it in **Section G.1 in Appendix**).

**About the kernel-based IV methods**: Thank you for your suggestions. We have implemented KernelIV (Singh et al., 2019) and DualIV (Muandet et al., 2019) and updated **Table 1,2,4,5,6 and Figure 2** in the revision. Besides, we also add continuous treatment simulation studies **Demand** in **Section F in Appendix** to compare our CB-IV with previous IV methods and Confounder Balance methods. The results show that our CB-IV method achieves the best performance on treatment effect estimation in most cases.

content.title: Response to Reviewer uVdE Comments (Part 2)
content.comment:
**About the performance in different sample size**: CB-IV relies on extensive samples to ensure performance and bound the expected treatment effect estimation error. As reported in **Figure 2**, although the proposed method already does very well in small sample sizes on average, the variance is enormous above small data sets ($<$3000). As the number of data increases, the variance of CB-IV will decrease continuously. When the amount of data exceeds 3000, the upper bound of CB-IV's error will be lower than the lower bound of all baselines. 

**About the performance of pure IV methods**: Comparing the confounder balance methods with the CB-IV in **Table 1,2,4,5,6 and Figure 2**, we have known that IV is a strong tool to address the unmeasured confounders. Based on your concerns, we adjust the difficulty of the simulation and add a classic continuous treatment simulation **Demand**, that reported in **Table 1 and 6**. From the results, we observe that the confounder balance methods without IV still perform much better than the pure IV based methods. We think it might be that the pure IV based methods suffer from the confounding bias from the treatment regression stage (observed confounders are used in stage 1). More details can be found in **Section F in Appendix**.

**About the OneSIV**: OneSIV has worse performance with the increase of sample size both in the binary treatment cases and continuous treatment cases, reported in **Table 5 and Figure 2**. In finite samples, OneSIV, without any regularization, combines losses from two stages into a multi-objective loss and tries to leverage the outcome information to estimate the treatment distribution. From the empirical experiments, we find that with increasing sample size, the prediction of treatment variables will become more accurate, but the confounding bias will increase. Even OneSIV may not converge if there is no regularization on the outcome regression model. Our CB-IV uses representation balancing regularization and two-head outcome functions to address this problem to obtain more accurate treatment estimation and better potential outcome estimation. 

**We have updated the paper to address your concerns; see the modified parts, marked in red**:

(i) We have corrected this part from “reduce bias” to “achieve better bias-variance trade-off” through our paper;

(ii) About more discussion on confounder balance: We add it in Section G in Appendix on pages 18-21; 

(iii) About the kernel-based IV methods: We have implemented KernelIV and DualIV, and updated Table 1 on page 8, Table 2 on page 9, Table 4 on page 18, Tables 5-6 on page 19, and Figure 2 on page 8 in the revision.

(iv) About the complex continuous treatment cases: We add it in Section F in Appendix on pages 17-18, Table 5 and Table 6 on page 19. 

Please forward any other thoughts, ideas, or concerns.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of treatment effect estimation in the presence of unmeasured confounders. The authors focus on an instrumental variable (IV) approach. Traditional IV approach requires strong assumptions, e.g., linearity or additivity. The paper aims at relaxing these stringent assumptions by proposing a Confounder Balanced IV Regression (CB-IV) algorithm. The proposed algorithm combines confounder balancing and IV regression. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm even without the additive separability assumption on noise.
content.main_review:
To the best of my knowledge, this paper is a novel combination of the confounder balancing and IV regression. The problem considered is a very important problem; the assumptions required by the classical IV method are strong, and it is important to relax them. I’m overall positive about the paper, but here are a few comments and questions I have.  

-	The authors mention many times in the paper that “effective even without the additive separability assumption on noise”. However, looking at equation (5), I think the form still looks “additive”. There do not appear to be interaction terms between U and X. I understand that having interaction terms between U and X could make things overly complicated, and I’m fine with this assumption, but it will be great if the assumptions can be explained and advocated more accurately. 
-	Related to the above point, can Y be written in the more general form of Y = g1(T,X) + g2(T,U)? If not, it will be great if we can see more explanation of this assumption. Why do you choose this form? Is it because of its generality or it is necessary for the theorems to go through?
-	We never really have a definition of h(T, X) in the paper. It is confusing what it really means. The first time it appears is in equation (2). 
-	Related to the above point, many notations appear earlier than their definitions. For example, g1, g2. They are used in equation (2) but not defined until (5). 
-	I think the term “confounder balancing” can be explained better. Currently it is only briefly explained in the related work section and section 3.3(2). It would be great if we can see: what does it mean by confounder balancing, why is it desirable, and how do we do this in the proposed algorithm.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the proposed method is new. The problem is considered in important. My overall comment is positive. But I think the results can be presented in a better way. The results also do not seem to be as strong as claimed by the author: “without the additive separability assumption”.

content.title: Response to Reviewer D2wS Comments
content.comment:
Thank you for your thought-provoking comment. Below, we address your concerns point by point. Please kindly let us know whether you have any further concerns.

**About the additive noise assumption and the structural model**: In Eq.(4) (Eq. (5) in original paper, now we revise it as Eq. (4) in revision), we relax the additive noise assumption ($T = f(Z,X)+U, Y = g(T,X)+U, U \sim N(0,\sigma^2)$) required in previous IV based methods, but we still need some structural assumption to precisely estimate the treatment effect, and we term it as the multiplicative assumption ($T = f_1(Z,X)+f_2(Z)f_3(X,U)$, $Y = g_1(T,X)+g_2(T)g_3(U)+g_4(X,U)$). We have revised the original description "without additive noise assumption" as "under the multiplicative assumption" in paper, marked in red. 

In addition, for $Y$, $Y = g_1(T,X) + g_2(T)*g_3(U)$ would be a better choice. Because $U$ cannot be used in the regression estimation of $Y$, it is difficult to discuss whether the complex entanglement  between $U$ and $T$ (e.g., $g(T,U)={1}_\mathrm{U<0,T>0}*g_U(U)+{1}_\mathrm{U<0,T \leq 0}*g_\mathrm{TU}(T, U)+{1}_\mathrm{U \geq 0}*g_T(T)$) will affect the regression of $Y$. Based on your suggestions, we generalize and redefine Eq.(4): for $T$, $T = f_1(Z,X) + f_2(Z) * f_3(X,U)$; for $Y$, $Y = g_1(T,X) + g_2(T) * g_3(U) + g_4(X,U)$, marked in red on page 4. The completeness of $P({T \mid Z,X})$ and $P({Y \mid T,X})$ guarantees the uniqueness of the solution (Newey & Powell, 2003).

**About the definition of h(T, X)**: Thanks for your suggestion. We have updated the manuscript and adjusted the structure of paper. In this paper, $Y = g_1(T,X) + g_2(T) * g_3(U) + g_4(X,U)$ is the structural function of $Y$, then we define the latent outcome prediction function as $h(T,X) = g_1(T,X)+g_2(T)\mathbb{E}[g_3(U)|C]+\mathbb{E}[g_4(X,U)|C]$ (similar definition can be found in Eq.(1) and (2) in Hartford et al., (2017)). 

**About the confounder balancing and why is it desirable**: In the outcome regression stage in IV-based methods, the predicted treatment $\hat{T}$, obtained from the treatment regression stage, suffers from confounding bias from the observed confounders $X$ (Figure 1(b)). In finite samples, the direct regression might be incorrect or overfitted on the limited biased data. Moreover, the treatment indicator might be get lost in direct regression due to the high-dimensional confounders. Thus, the **confounder balancing** can be seen as a type of regularization on the regression model, that means we try to balance the distributions of confounders $X$ between different treatment arms $\hat{T}$ to simulate the results of Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs), i.e., converting $\mathbb{P}(X|\hat{T}_1) \ne \mathbb{P}(X|\hat{T}_0)$ to $\mathbb{P}(f_\theta(X)| \hat{T}_1)=\mathbb{P}(f_\theta(X)| \hat{T}_0)=\mathbb{P}(f_\theta(X))$. More details can be found in **Section G.1 in Appendix**, we use a hospital example combined with Randomized Controlled Trials to illustrate it. 

**About how to balance representation**: CFR (Shalit et al., 2017) proves that the "balanced" representation will help to bound the expected treatment effect estimation error: $\epsilon(h, \Phi) \leq 2\left(\epsilon_{F}^{t=0}(h, \Phi)+\epsilon_{F}^{t=1}(h, \Phi)+B_{\Phi} I P M_{\mathrm{G}}\left(p_{\Phi}^{t=1}, p_{\Phi}^{t=0}\right)-2 \sigma_{Y}^{2}\right)$. In binary treatment cases, we use Wasserstein distance (Wass) to calculate the dissimilarity of distributions from different treatment arms and fit a balanced representation by minimizing the discrepancy. As for continuous cases, we minimize the mutual information between the treatment $T$ and the representation $C$ to make them independent of each other, i.e., $T \perp C$.

**We have updated the paper to address your concerns; see the modified parts, marked in red**:

(i) About the additive noise assumption and the structural model: We have revised the original description "without additive noise assumption" as "under the multiplicative assumption" in paper, and revised the Eq.(4) (Eq. (5) in original paper) on page 4;

(ii) About the definition of $h(T, X)$: We adjust and place it on page 4; 

(iii) About the more discussion on confounder balance: We add it in Section G in Appendix on pages 18-21. 

Please forward any other thoughts, ideas, or concerns.

display_title: Official Review of Paper304 by Reviewer DjHx

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on the average treatment effect estimation with instrumental variables with nonlinear outcome model and no additive noise assumptions. The paper proposes a three-step method Confounder Balanced IV (CB-IV) Regression, where the confounder balance step addresses observed confounders and the instrumental variable deals with unobserved confounders. In the provided numerical experiments, the proposed method is shown to successfully remove the bias.
content.main_review:
The paper raises an interesting bias problem in non-linear IV methods with valid practical implications. The paper identifies different roles of unobserved and observed confounders and removes the two sources of bias combining confounder balance and instrumental variable.
 
It would be very nice of the authors to provide more explanations to the points below.

(1) The structural model (Eq.(5)) seems a bit unnatural/stringent to me. I could think of a few alternatives without the additive noise assumption, e.g., for T, T = f_1(Z,X) + f_2(X,U) + f_3(Z,U), and for Y: Y = g_1(T,X) + g_2(X,U) + g_3(T,U). Could you please provide some references or motivations of using Eq.(5)?

(2) The second step of the optimization (Confounder Balancing) minimizes the Wasserstein distance. It would be very helpful to provide some intuitions of the choice over integral probability metrics.

(3) The authors state in the conclusion that "The same framework is also applicable to continuous treatment variables, but the conditional independent constraint of continuous variables is still an open problem..." If I understand correctly, the difficulty lies in finding the conditionally independent representation. In Section 3.3, the authors mentioned previous works using mutual information for confounder balancing given continuous treatments. I am wondering why the mutual information criterion does not solve the continuous treatment case in the CB-IV framework?
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem of the paper is well-motivated and the approach serves the goal. I am currently a bit concerned about the generality of the developed CB-IV approach, in particular, the model assumption (Eq.(5)) and the difficulty in applying it to continuous treatments.

In addition, for some function families, there is no known way or a simple method to compute the integral probability metric or its gradients efficiently. Wass distance has consistent estimators, which can be efficiently computed in the finite sample case (Shalit et al., 2017; Sriperumbudur et al., 2012). Besides, Wass distance is a common measure in deep learning, and many algorithm breakthroughs (Arjovsky et al., 2017; Cuturi & Doucet, 2014) benefit from it.

**About continuous treatment cases**: Thank you for the constructive feedback. The mutual information criterion can solve the continuous treatment case in the CB-IV framework. Based on your suggestions, we added the continuous treatment experiments in **Section F in Appendix**. In addition, we have added some baselines (e.g., KernelIV and DualIV) for comparisons. For continuous treatment case Demand (that applied in DeepIV (Hartford et al., 2017), KernelIV (Singh et al., 2019),DualIV (Muandet et al., 2019) and DFIV (Xu et al., 2020)), we report mean squared error (MSE) and its standard deviations over 10 trials with different data size (500, 1000, 5000, 10000). The results demonstrate that our method CB-IV improved considerably over the traditional IV-based methods and achieved better performance than confounder balancing methods in most settings, especially on large samples.

**We have updated the paper to address your concerns; see the modified parts, marked in red**:

(i) About the additive noise assumption and the structural model: We have revised the original description "without additive noise assumption" as "under the multiplicative assumption" in paper, and revised the Eq.(4) (Eq. (5) in original paper) on page 4;

(ii) About the Wass distance: We add it in Section G.2 in Appendix on pages 20-21; 

(iii) About the continuous treatment cases: We add it in Section F in Appendix on pages 17-18, Table 5 and Table 6 on page 19. 

Please forward any other thoughts, ideas, or concerns.
